stops.name: Macerata, the apothecary's son
stops.campa: Matteo Ricci is born in Macerata, in the Marche, the eldest of thirteen children of Giovanni Battista Ricci, apothecary and sometime governor of the town, and Giovanna Angiolelli. He is baptized within days in the cathedral font. The family house stands within the old walls, near the piazza where his father will one day serve as gonfaloniere. Nothing yet marks him for the far side of the earth; he is simply a merchant's son in a hill town of the Papal States, a childhood no different in its outward shape from a thousand others of the Marche.

stops.name: Macerata, the Jesuit school on the Piaggia
stops.campa: At nine Ricci enters the newly founded Jesuit school in Macerata, one of the first colleges the Society opens in the Papal States. He studies grammar, rhetoric and Christian doctrine under masters trained in the pedagogy Ignatius Loyola has only lately set down, and shows a quickness his teachers remark on. It is here, among the black cassocks and the ratio studiorum still taking shape, that the rest of his life is first cut, though neither he nor his father yet intends the cloth for him; the apothecary means his son for the law.

stops.name: Rome, the law student turns from La Sapienza
stops.campa: Sent to Rome at sixteen to study law at La Sapienza, as his father intends, Ricci instead falls under the gravity of the Society of Jesus, whose houses stand thick about the university quarter. He haunts the Jesuit church of Sant'Andrea, drawn to the discipline and the learning more than to the courts. His father, hearing of the drift, is said to have set out for Rome to reclaim him for the family trade; a fever on the road stops him, and he takes it, the story runs, as a sign not to interfere with his son's calling.

stops.name: Rome, admitted to the Society of Jesus at Sant'Andrea al Quirinale
stops.campa: On the feast of the Assumption, Ricci enters the Society's novitiate on the Quirinal hill, the ground where Bernini's Sant'Andrea will rise a century after him, and puts off the law for good, taking the vows of poverty, chastity and obedience that will carry him, though none can yet foresee it, to the far side of Asia. The Society at this hour is barely thirty years old and already reaching past every horizon its founder knew; Ricci is one more recruit to a project that treats the whole world, China included, as its field of harvest.

stops.name: Rome, the Collegio Romano and the mathematics of Father Clavius
stops.campa: At the Collegio Romano, the Society's flagship school, Ricci studies philosophy and theology, but it is the mathematics classroom of Christoph Clavius, architect of the calendar reform Rome will promulgate within a decade, that marks him deepest. He learns Euclid's geometry, spherical astronomy, cosmography, and the making of instruments, sundials, astrolabes, striking clocks, none of which he can know he will one day trade for entry into the confidence of the Ming court. Clavius's method, proof built rigorously on proof, becomes the frame Ricci will carry, whole, into a language that has no word yet for it.

stops.name: Rome, chosen for the Indies
stops.campa: Ricci petitions the Father General for the Indies mission and is chosen among the volunteers, part of the great outward push Francis Xavier began a generation before. In May he leaves Rome for Genoa and the overland road to Lisbon, the single door through which the Portuguese Padroado lets missionaries pass east. He carries almost nothing but his training: languages, mathematics, the habits of a Jesuit scholastic not yet ordained. Behind him lies every certainty of Italy; ahead, a passage no one has told him will end, decades on, in a city called Peking.

stops.name: Coimbra, waiting on the fleet
stops.campa: At the Jesuit college of Coimbra, staging ground for the whole Portuguese Asian mission, Ricci waits out the months before the India fleet sails, sharpening his Portuguese and his theology among Jesuits bound for Goa, Malacca and Japan. Coimbra has sent missionaries east for thirty years already; its corridors are hung with the names of those who did not return. He is one recruit among many funneled through this single narrow gate, the Padroado's chokepoint, before the Atlantic and the whole turning world beyond it.

stops.name: Lisbon, the Tagus, departure
stops.campa: On the twenty-fourth of March Ricci sails from Lisbon down the Tagus and past the tower of Belém with the annual India fleet under the Visitor Alessandro Valignano, who will shape the whole of the Jesuit mission to the Far East. Thirteen companions travel with him; the carrack is provisioned for half a year and bound around the whole of Africa on the Carreira da Índia, the sea road the Portuguese have held for eighty years. Few aboard have any assurance they will see Europe again, and Ricci does not.

stops.name: Rounding the Cape, five months at sea
stops.campa: The fleet rounds the Cape of Storms deep in the southern winter, the stretch of the passage Portuguese sailors fear most of all. Provisions rot, water sours, and the fevers and scurvy that kill a fixed fraction of every India crossing move through the lower decks; Jesuit chroniclers of the Carreira routinely bury shipmates before Mozambique. Ricci keeps to his theology and his instruments as much as the pitching hull allows, one more soul on a five-month crossing the Portuguese themselves call, without much exaggeration, the graveyard route.

stops.name: Goa, landfall in the Estado da Índia
stops.campa: Ricci makes landfall at Goa, capital of the Estado da Índia and the Jesuits' great eastern seminary, after nearly six months at sea. He completes his theological studies here and teaches the humanities to younger students; for a period he loses the use of his eyes so completely to strain and fever that his superiors fear he will never read again. He recovers, and treats the recovery, in the language of the mission, as a mercy meant to keep him for greater use. Goa is the hinge of the whole Portuguese East, the port from which every road to China, Japan or the Moluccas departs.

stops.name: Cochin, ordained priest
stops.campa: Sent south to Cochin for his health, Ricci is ordained to the priesthood in the summer of 1580, the sacrament that completes his long Jesuit formation and licenses the work he does not yet know awaits him. He says his first Masses among the Malabar Christians and the Portuguese garrison of the pepper coast, still recovering his strength, still without any certainty that China, closed to missionaries for a generation, will ever open to him. He returns north to Goa a full priest of the Society, waiting on Valignano's summons.

stops.name: Macau, summoned to the edge of the Middle Kingdom
stops.campa: Valignano recalls Ricci from Goa to Macau, the single Portuguese toehold on the Chinese coast and the mission's forward post against an empire that has expelled or refused every missionary sent against its gates. Here Ricci joins Michele Ruggieri, already laboring at the language no European has yet mastered, in a school built for exactly one purpose: to produce a priest China itself cannot easily throw out, because he speaks and reads as a Chinese scholar does. Valignano's wager is total inculturation, and Macau is the last rehearsal before the gate.
